MSK-SKIN · WEEK 18 · THURSDAY LECTURE 1

Exercise is Medicine

Lecture Companion · Chris Ledford, MD, CAQSM · November 19, 2026

← Week 18Factoid Sheet →ObjectivesEvidenceCounselingOsteoarthritisFITT–VP & safetyMaster review

Learning objectives

  1. Discuss efficacy of exercise as medicine in preventing and treating disease.
  2. Discuss the physician’s role in promoting exercise as a routine part of clinical practice.
  3. Identify exercises that can improve pain and function in common MSK disorders (e.g., osteoarthritis).
  4. Safely apply components of an exercise prescription to a patient with common MSK disorders (e.g., osteoarthritis).
Big picture. Exercise is a measurable therapeutic exposure, not simply advice to be active. First identify what the patient already does, then choose an appropriate dose, account for joint symptoms and medical risk, and help the patient sustain the plan. The biggest opportunity may be moving an inactive patient toward even modest activity.

1 · Exercise in disease prevention and treatment

Slides 2–15, 23–24, 44

Why inactivity matters

The WHO historical chart ranks physical inactivity among major contributors to global deaths (fourth in the 2004 comparison). A separate 2007 figure assigns 40% of premature deaths to behavioral patterns, compared with genetic predisposition 30%, social circumstances 15%, health care 10% and environmental exposure 5%. This is a population attribution estimate, not a prediction for an individual. The lecture highlights Georgia: 27.9% report no leisure-time activity; in 2019, 49.1% achieved the aerobic target. The obesity map (BRFSS 2025, ages 40–59) reinforces the public-health context; these are historical slide data, not newly verified surveillance.

Definitions: behavior, structured training and capacity

TermMeaningExample
Physical activity (PA)Skeletal muscle contraction raises energy expenditure substantially above restWalking to class
ExercisePlanned, structured, repetitive PA intended to improve or maintain fitnessScheduled cycling sessions
Physical fitnessAttributes that determine the capacity to perform PAAerobic exercise capacity
COMMON CONFUSION Exercise is a subset of PA; fitness is a capacity, not the behavior itself.
Intensity (slide 10)METsExamples
Light<3Slow walk, croquet
Moderate3 to <63 mph walk, walking golf pulling clubs, doubles tennis
Vigorous>6 (slide wording)4.5 mph very brisk walk 6.3; 5 mph jog or singles tennis 8; digging 8.5; competitive soccer 10
EXAM TRAP Slide 10 uses >6 for vigorous, while the AMI figure on slide 42 uses ≥6. The exact 6-MET boundary is inconsistent; standard categorization usually starts vigorous at 6 METs (board/clinical clarification).

Fitness and mortality show an inverse association. The graph does not prove that all of the difference is caused by training; it emphasizes the opportunity to improve the lowest fitness category. For ASCVD, the cited study reports a 26% lower CHD risk per 50 MET-h/week higher activity; quoted comparisons include running (42%) and brisk walking (18%). Exercise-related lipid profile changes (LDL/HDL) were reported independently of adherence to the AHA diet in the cited study.

FIRST AID CONNECTION · p. 289–291 Exercise raises contractility and stroke volume; cardiac output = HR × SV. As stroke volume plateaus at higher workloads, further output increases depend more on HR. Exercise also lowers total peripheral resistance. This links workload to cardiovascular demand.
FOUNDATIONS LINK METs express intensity; multiplying intensity by duration estimates the accumulated dose. Fitness is not the same as total weekly activity.

Exercise versus medication: interpret the evidence

The lecture cites a network meta-analysis of 16 meta-analyses (305 studies, 339,274 participants; 4 exercise and 12 drug meta-analyses), assessing mortality in CHD, stroke, heart failure and prediabetes.

HIGH YIELD Exercise can be a meaningful treatment component, but this figure does not justify withdrawing indicated medications or claiming that exercise is superior for every disease.

Cancer prevention and survivorship

Strong evidence for lower incidence is also listed for bladder (15%), endometrial (20%), esophageal adenocarcinoma (21%), gastric (19%), renal (12%) and lung (21–25%) cancers. Evidence is limited or variable for several other cancers. In cancer treatment, activity may reduce pain and fatigue; aerobic exercise is emphasized for fatigue. The lecture recommends implementing a prescription before treatment or during survivorship.

Retrieval checkpoint · Which patient has the greatest potential mortality-risk improvement suggested by the fitness graph?

The least-fit patient moving into the next fitness category; the plot shows the largest absolute difference there.

2 · Physician’s role: make activity a routine clinical intervention

Slides 16–26

Knowing exercise is beneficial is different from helping someone do it. Physician advice plus written education had a sustained effect at six months (1 kcal/kg/day activity difference); the cited lecture associates that difference with 25% lower mortality. The lecture also notes a relationship between clinicians’ own activity and activity counseling.

Assess → advise → refer

Use the Exercise is Medicine (ACSM) approach: assess current activity routinely, give brief advice and/or a written exercise prescription, and refer for appropriate support or resources. Behavioral counseling may involve repeated contacts, motivational interviewing, goal setting, problem solving and self-monitoring. Slide 18 describes combined diet/activity interventions with a median of 12 contacts and about 6 contact hours over 6–18 months; activity counseling in the cited interventions aimed for 90–180 min/week moderate-to-vigorous activity.

MUST KNOW Aerobic target: 150 min/week moderate OR 75 min/week vigorous OR equivalent combination. One vigorous minute counts as two moderate minutes. The general PAVS slide allows bouts of any length; even light activity is beneficial although not counted by PAVS.

Example: a patient walks briskly for 20 min on three days and jogs for 15 min on two days. Their moderate-equivalent total is 60 + 2 × 30 = 120 min/week. They are 30 moderate-equivalent minutes below the target. Give an achievable next step rather than an all-or-nothing instruction.

Retrieval checkpoint · A patient walks briskly 4 days per week for 25 minutes. What is the PAVS and how far below target are they?

100 min/week, 50 moderate minutes below the 150-minute target.

3 · Exercise for osteoarthritis: improve pain and function

Slides 27–30, 35, 38–39

The 2015 Cochrane knee OA review found improvement in pain and function comparable in magnitude to NSAID effects, immediately after exercise treatment and during 2–6 month follow-up. It is not a claim that exercise and NSAIDs have identical mechanisms or risks.

Both aerobic and strengthening exercise are essential components; prescriptions should be individualized to age, comorbidity, mobility and patient preferences. Few contraindications are described for hip/knee OA exercise itself, but safety screening still applies. Group and home exercise are both effective; adherence is a major predictor of long-term outcome. Use monitoring, review and family support when helpful. The consensus table marks independence from radiographic severity as not recommended (insufficient basis for that proposition); it does not establish that imaging alone determines exercise benefit. Reduced disease progression from improved strength/proprioception is only a lower-grade recommendation.

HIGH YIELD Evidence categories: 1A = meta-analysis of randomized trials; 1B = ≥1 randomized trial; 2A = controlled trial without randomization; 2B = quasi-experimental study; 3 = descriptive study; 4 = expert opinion. Recommendation A is directly supported by category 1 evidence; B–D progressively reflect lower-level evidence or extrapolation.
FIRST AID CONNECTION · p. 472 OA: chronic mechanical stress → articular cartilage degeneration with inadequate repair → pain after use, relief with rest; asymmetric joint-space narrowing, osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis/cysts. RA instead involves autoimmune synovitis/pannus, prolonged morning stiffness improving with use, symmetric involvement and erosions. OA pain with activity does not mean appropriately dosed therapeutic movement is contraindicated.
BOARD / CLINICAL ENRICHMENT Low-impact modes limit peak joint loading; strengthening increases muscular support, and flexibility maintains available motion. Isometric contraction creates muscle tension without appreciable joint movement, allowing an initial strengthening option when motion is painful.
Exercise modeWhat to chooseReasoning
AerobicWalking, cycling, pool exerciseStart lower impact to build tolerance
ResistanceAll major muscle groups; concentric and eccentric; isometric if pain-limitedStrength and function
FlexibilityMajor groups daily, warm-up/cool-downMaintain mobility
MSK CONNECTION Concentric = muscle shortens under tension; eccentric = lengthens under tension; isometric = tension without appreciable length change. Select the contraction type based on the patient’s tolerance.
Retrieval checkpoint · A patient with knee OA has pain with repetitive knee bending. Which initial resistance mode might help?

Isometric exercises, because they generate muscle tension with minimal joint movement.

4 · Prescribe exercise safely: FITT–VP

Slides 31–43

ComponentLecture OA prescription
FrequencyAerobic 3–5 d/wk; resistance 2–3 d/wk, preferably nonconsecutive; flexibility daily if possible.
Intensity40–60% age-predicted maximum HR; sedentary target conflicts between slides 33 and 37.
TimeAt least 150 min/wk moderate or 75 min/wk vigorous; accumulate shorter bouts.
TypeLow-impact walking, cycling, water activity; all major muscle groups; isometric initially if pain limits movement; daily flexibility.
VolumeTotal exercise dose (MET-min/wk); 150 min at 4 METs = 600 MET-min/wk (illustration).
ProgressionAdd 5–10 min/wk aerobic activity toward goal; resistance may increase 10%/wk by reps or weight; adapt to pain lasting 2 h.
COMMON CONFUSION · source discrepancy Slide 33 gives 50–60% of age-predicted max HR for deconditioned/sedentary patients; slide 37 gives 30–40%. Both state 40–60% generally. Do not silently substitute one. Confirm the expected examination range with the lecturer. The lecture also gives 10-minute bouts in slides 34/37, 5-minute bouts if better tolerated in slide 36, and any-length bouts in the general PAVS slide 25.

Worked example: target heart rate

Age-predicted maximum HR = 220 − age. For a 55-year-old: 165 bpm × 0.60 = 99 bpm (lecture example). The general 40–60% range would be 66–99 bpm. This is the percentage of predicted maximum HR, not heart-rate reserve.

BOARD / CLINICAL ENRICHMENT Age-predicted HR is an estimate; beta blockers and other factors may blunt HR response. Use patient symptoms and the talk test as additional guides; this is not a standalone exercise clearance method.

Progression and practical counseling

  • Pain still present two hours after a session → consider altering the activity.
  • General FITT–VP slide: advance by 5–10 minutes every 1–2 weeks for 4–6 weeks. OA-specific slide: add 5–10 minutes weekly toward 150 min/week; resistance may increase 10% per week in repetitions or weight.
  • Replace athletic shoes every 300–500 miles or 300 hours; at least annually even with less use (lecture advice).
  • Pool temperature 83–88°F may improve relaxation and reduce pain.
  • If taking pain medication, time activity around peak effect as advised in the lecture; do not increase dosing just to exercise.
  • Moderate intensity: talk but cannot sing; vigorous: difficult to talk, somewhat breathless.

Safety: habitual activity and acute exertion

CLINICAL CONNECTION Regular activity is associated with lower risk, but sudden vigorous exercise in an untrained patient creates a disproportionately large short-term risk. Start low and progress gradually rather than prescribing immediate vigorous exercise.

Preparticipation screening

First ask whether the patient already participates in regular exercise, then assess known cardiovascular, metabolic or renal disease and any suggestive symptoms. The original slide uses all three to determine clearance.

Regular exercise?Clinical statusClearanceAction
NoNo known CV, metabolic or renal disease; no symptomsNo clearance necessaryLight–moderate; gradual progression
NoKnown CV, metabolic or renal disease; asymptomaticClearance recommendedAfter clearance, light–moderate; progress gradually
NoSymptoms suggestive of CV, metabolic or renal disease, regardless of diagnosisClearance recommendedAfter clearance, light–moderate; progress gradually
YesNo known disease; no symptomsNo clearance necessaryContinue moderate or vigorous; progress gradually
YesKnown disease; asymptomaticNot necessary for moderate; clearance recommended before vigorous (within last 12 months if unchanged)Continue moderate; progress after clearance
YesSuggestive symptoms, regardless of diagnosisDiscontinue exercise; seek clearanceReturn after clearance; progress gradually
Retrieval checkpoint · An inactive patient with known metabolic disease and no symptoms wants to start training. Clearance?

Recommended before starting; after clearance, light–moderate exercise with gradual progression.

Retrieval checkpoint · An already active patient develops symptoms suggestive of cardiovascular disease. What next?

Discontinue exercise and seek medical clearance, regardless of known disease status.

Adapt to comorbid conditions (slide 44)

ConditionLecture recommendation
HIVAerobic activity at low/moderate/high intensity does not negatively affect immune function or progression at any stage; physician clearance recommended in the lecture due to treatment-associated CV risk.
CancerExercise for pain/fatigue; aerobic exercise emphasized for fatigue; prescription before treatment or in survivorship.
Depression/anxietyYoga as mono- or adjunctive therapy shows positive effects particularly in depression; adjunctive yoga for anxiety, especially panic disorder; mindfulness as adjunct; activity associated with lower depression risk.
FIRST AID CONNECTION · p. 496 NSAIDs reversibly inhibit COX-1/COX-2 → ↓ prostaglandins → analgesia and anti-inflammatory effect; reduced protective prostaglandins explain gastric ulceration and renal ischemia. Exercise is a complementary nonpharmacologic tool, not an automatic replacement.

Apply the full prescription

Teaching case: A 55-year-old with knee OA, not regularly active and without known CV/metabolic/renal disease or suggestive symptoms, wants to improve walking tolerance. Under the slide 43 screening algorithm, clearance is not required solely for this profile. Start with tolerable low-impact walking or cycling in short bouts, perhaps 5–10 min on 3 days/week; aim gradually toward 150 min/week, use the talk test and individualized intensity, add resistance 2–3 nonconsecutive days and daily flexibility. Monitor symptoms after each session. The initial duration is an illustrative teaching choice, not a universal prescription. The conflicting sedentary HR ranges should be clarified rather than treated as settled.

Retrieval checkpoint · If knee pain persists two hours after the session, what should change?

Consider reducing or altering intensity, duration or mode rather than automatically progressing.

Master these before moving on

  1. PA vs exercise vs fitness: behavior, structured behavior and capacity are distinct; this separates dose from outcome.
  2. Moderate-equivalent minutes: vigorous minutes count twice; use the PAVS to identify a practical target.
  3. OA exercise: low-impact aerobic + strengthening + flexibility; tailor and prioritize adherence, not immobility.
  4. FITT–VP: specify all six variables and progress based on tolerance.
  5. Screening: habitual activity, known disease and symptoms determine whether clearance is needed; new concerning symptoms require evaluation.

Most useful First Aid connections

  • p. 472: OA mechanical pain, asymmetric narrowing and osteophytes vs RA inflammatory stiffness and erosions.
  • pp. 289–291: cardiac output and contractility during exercise, reduced peripheral resistance.
  • p. 496: NSAID COX inhibition, GI and renal toxicity.

Source: Chris Ledford, MD, “Exercise is Medicine,” Nov 19, 2026, slides 1–45. First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 2025, printed pages as listed (PDF pages 310–312, 493, 517).
